title: ⭐ Practice: naming a disaster, and choosing a future

questions.prompt: A geologist explains that lava, steam and ash are forced out through an opening in the earth's crust, sometimes continuously and sometimes at long intervals. Which of the five disasters of your module is he defining?
questions.explanation: Your book defines a volcano as a vent — a hole — in the earth's crust through which lava, steam and ash are expelled, either continuously or at irregular intervals, which is the definition word for word. An earthquake also happens in the crust, but it is a series of vibrations set off when strained rocks break and rebound abruptly, and nothing is forced out of the ground. A flood is water flowing or overflowing over land. A tsunami is the tempting answer, because an undersea volcanic eruption is one of the two things that produce one — but the tsunami is the wave itself, not the opening the eruption came through.

questions.prompt: Amine decided last week to plant a row of young trees behind his school, and the trees are already bought and standing in his yard. On Thursday a friend asks him what he is doing on Saturday. Which answer states the plan he made before?

options.text: I am going plant them there.
I plant them there every Saturday.

questions.explanation: be going to announces a plan formed before the moment of speaking, and the situation gives you both marks of one: the decision was taken last week and the trees are already bought. will belongs to a decision taken as you speak — an offer, a promise, something you settle on the spot — so "I will plant them, then" would mean the idea came to him while his friend was still asking. The plain present with every Saturday states a habit and turns one afternoon's work into a weekly routine. And "I am going plant them there" drops the to that be going to always carries: the form is going to plant, never "going plant".

questions.prompt: A walker finds a mountain hut with the door open and a cup of tea still warm on the table. Nobody is inside. He says to himself: "Somebody ___ this hut a few minutes ago."
questions.explanation: He did not see anybody go; he concludes it from the warm cup, and a conclusion about something already over takes must followed by have and a past participle: somebody must have left. must leave draws its conclusion about now, or else lays down an obligation, and the person he is talking about is already gone. must be leaving describes an action going on at this very moment, and the hut is empty. And must left is the fault to watch for: a modal is always followed by a base form, so the past cannot sit on the verb itself — it is carried by the participle after have.

questions.prompt: In the days after a hurricane, while the streets were still under water, some people broke into the empty shops and carried the goods away. Which verb of your module names what they did?
questions.explanation: To loot is to steal goods, by force, in the disorder that follows a disaster, and the people who do it are looters — the word your survivor's account uses of those who profited by the chaotic situation to take away goods and furniture. To grab is to take something roughly, which is part of what they did, but it says nothing about whose the goods were: a rescuer grabs a rope, and the word would fit him just as well. To perish is to die. To yell is to cry out loudly in fright.

questions.prompt: A report on the mudslide is being written: "The heavy rain of the previous week ___ the collapse of the hillside." Which verb puts the rain in the place of the cause?
questions.explanation: To bring something about is to cause it, so the rain does the causing and the collapse is what follows: the rain brought about the collapse. resulted from turns the sentence round, since a thing results from its own cause — the sentence would then claim that a week of rain was produced by a hillside falling down. (The verb that would work in that slot is result in: the rain resulted in the collapse.) came from names an origin, a place or a source rather than a cause, and it would make the collapse the country the rain came out of. depended on says that one thing varies with another, not that one produced the other.

questions.prompt: Four people are told the same thing: a factory has been pouring its waste straight into the river for years. One of them expresses shock and dismay; the other three do not. Which one?
questions.explanation: Your book's table keeps That's awful! for shock and dismay, beside Oh, no!, How shocking!, That's terrible! and That's horrible! — the reply of somebody who has taken the news in and condemns it. Really? and I didn't know that. sit in the first column, mild surprise or interest: they report that the fact is new to the listener and judge it in no way at all. You're joking! belongs to the middle column, strong surprise and disbelief, and there is the distinction the exercise is built on — it says you find the news hard to believe, so it questions the fact instead of condemning it. Say it to somebody who has just given you a figure he stands by, and you have told him you think he is wrong.
